title: Secure egress patterns for private inference
content:
Purpose and audience:
This is a compact reference for solutions engineers and customer infra teams running Redwood Private or Dedicated in VPCs. The doc summarizes recommended egress/ingress/DNS patterns for inference workloads that need strict data exfiltration controls or constrained outbound connectivity (PCI/PHI/Restricted SaaS environments). Use as a workshop handout and as a checklist for handoff to customer networking teams.

Context and constraints we commonly see:
- Customer does not want any uncontrolled egress to the public internet from inference nodes.
- Some customers allow TLS-only egress to a small set of vendor endpoints (e.g., model download, metrics, license checks).
- Auditors often require full URL allowlists, egress proxying, and TLS inspection point details.
- Private deployments may be air-gapped for model weights; then control plane calls are proxied through an approved gateway.

High-level patterns (pros/cons):
1) Egress-through-central-proxy (recommended default)
   - Pattern: All worker subnets route 0.0.0.0/0 to a central NAT/proxy VPC (transit or shared services). Proxy performs allowlisting, logging, and can TLS-terminate if required.
   - Pros: Centralized logging and controls; single place for auditor signoff. Easy to attach IDS/IPS.
   - Cons: Single failure domain unless highly available. Adds latency for small downstream calls (model telemetry, license).

2) Service endpoints + private links (for cloud-managed partners)
   - Pattern: Use cloud provider private endpoints (AWS PrivateLink, Azure Private Endpoint) for curated services (S3-compatible storage, metrics/telemetry, private model stores).
   - Pros: No public egress for supported services, lower attack surface. Good for compliance.
   - Cons: Requires partner support or proxying of services that lack private endpoints. Additional VPC endpoint costs.

3) Scoped egress via egress firewall appliances (appliance per AZ)
   - Pattern: Deploy lightweight egress appliances (eBPF-based or third-party firewall) in each AZ to enforce per-subnet allowlists.
   - Pros: Lower cross-AZ traffic, can be cheaper at scale.
   - Cons: More operational overhead; rolling upgrades across AZs during changes.

4) Zero-egress (air-gapped) with controlled model sync
   - Pattern: Inference plane has zero outbound network. Model and metrics sync happens via a scheduled, credentialed bastion or offline transfer process.
   - Pros: Strongest compliance posture.
   - Cons: Operationally heavy; difficult for telemetry and real-time fallbacks. Not suitable for hosted API features that require ongoing callbacks.

DNS strategies (split-horizon, resolver placement):
- Use split-horizon DNS when customers need different resolutions for the same hostname inside vs outside the VPC (e.g., internal S3-compatible object store vs public S3). Run an internal Route53 private hosted zone (or equivalent) and ensure worker subnets point to internal resolvers.
- For egress via proxy, ensure DNS resolution happens inside the VPC (do not leak DNS to public resolvers). Configure DHCP options or instance metadata to point to the internal resolver.
- Consider forwarding rules so internal DNS can resolve vendor hostnames to private endpoints when PrivateLink is configured.

Decision matrix for choosing a pattern:
- Compliance level: PCI/PHI/High -> favor private endpoints or zero-egress.
- Ops maturity: Small infra team -> central proxy.
- Latency sensitivity: Real-time inference -> avoid cross-AZ backhauls; prefer local appliances or PrivateLink.
- Cost constraints: PrivateLink and per-AZ appliances may add direct cost; central NAT can be cheaper but increases data egress fees.

Hands-on workshop checklist (to run with customer networking team):
- [ ] Inventory: list CIDR ranges for inference subnets, control plane subnets, and any existing shared-services VPCs.
- [ ] Allowed endpoints: collect fully qualified hostnames/IPs for model registries, metrics endpoints, license servers.
- [ ] DNS plan: decide on private hosted zones, forwarding chains, and whether split-horizon is needed.
- [ ] Egress mechanism: choose one (central proxy, PrivateLink, per-AZ appliance, air-gap).
- [ ] TLS strategy: terminates at proxy? passthrough? do we need TLS inspection certs?
- [ ] Audit logging: where will egress logs be stored (S3/bigquery) and who will own retention?
- [ ] HA plan: NAT/proxy scaling, multi-AZ, failover tests.
- [ ] Security controls: IPS/IDS options, host hardening, eBPF-based L7 controls if needed.
- [ ] Handover doc: provide runbook for rotating creds and for emergency revoke of vendor endpoints.

Sample AWS-specific implementation notes (quick sketches):
- Central proxy pattern (AWS):
  - Create a shared-services VPC with an AutoScaling group of proxy instances behind an ALB/NLB. Route inference subnets' default route via Transit Gateway attachment to shared-services VPC.
  - Use AWS IAM roles tied to instance profiles for proxy nodes to push logs to CloudWatch/S3.
  - Add CloudWatch agent + Fluentd on proxies for detailed URL-level logging (if legal).

- PrivateLink pattern (AWS):
  - For model store: deploy an NLB in the partner VPC, expose as VPCE service. Create interface endpoints in customer VPC. Update security groups to allow endpoint ENIs to talk to model store.
  - For S3: use gateway endpoints to avoid NAT for bucket access.

Operational pitfalls we've hit in POCs (real notes):
- Customers sometimes provide only IP allowlists for initial tests. These break quickly because vendor hostnames change CDNs or IP ranges. Strongly prefer FQDN allowlists plus monitoring.
- Over-reliance on single proxy AZ caused outages when proxy ASG scaled slowly under bursty download traffic (model downloads). Set pre-warming and health checks.
- Split-horizon DNS misconfigurations that allowed internal instances to resolve to public IPs (sneaky and causes undetected egress). Make internal resolvers authoritative for sensitive names.

Unresolved questions to raise in next CST workshop:
- Does the customer accept TLS SNI-based allowlisting (SNI inspection) or require full URL logging?
- Are there business requirements to allow inbound callbacks to the inference plane (webhook model)? If yes, how are ingress firewalls expected to be configured?
- For audit evidence, does the customer need per-request payload sampling or is header-level metadata sufficient?

Emergency incident play (short):
- If we need to immediately cut all external telemetry: revoke the proxy security group egress rules, update route table to blackhole 0.0.0.0/0 for worker subnets, and trigger on-call. Have a pre-staged IAM role to remove vendor credentials.

Handover artifacts we provide to customers (deliverables):
- JSON/YAML sample route table and SG templates (CloudFormation/Terraform) for the chosen pattern.
- Small bash/Python scripts to validate egress (DNS checks, curl to allowlisted hosts, certificate pinning test).
- A one-page runbook for incidents (what to toggle in <5 mins).

Practical snippets (for workshop copy/paste):
- Sample DNS test (bash):
  curl -s --resolve api.vendor.local:443:10.0.4.12 https://api.vendor.local/healthz -I
- Simple connectivity validation (python):
  import socket
  sock = socket.create_connection(("api.metrics.vendor", 443), timeout=5)

Notes-to-self (informal):
- Push example Terraform for PrivateLink + Proxy reference when back at desk.
- Ask security about acceptable log retention windows; default to 90d for POC.
- Remind dev-rel to get vendor contact who can sign off on private endpoint changes.

Appendix: quick decision cheat-sheet (single line rules)
- Need zero public egress -> Air-gap + scheduled sync.
- Need low-latency outbound to vendor -> PrivateLink or local appliance.
- Need simple ops and central audit -> Central proxy via TGW/shared-services.

End of doc.
